# Stern-Gerlach and quantum spin states

{{< iconify lucide construction >}} this page is under construction {{< iconify lucide construction >}}

The striking thing about this chapter, for me, is not the physics of the Stern-Gerlach
experiment itself — it's that once the dust settles, the mathematics is *identical* to
[the Jones-vector story](jones_vectors.qmd). Same two-component complex columns, same
invisibility of overall phase and scale, same $SU(2)$ rotation group, same angle-doubling.
Two completely different physical setups (a classical EM wave through crystal optics,
and a beam of silver atoms through an inhomogeneous magnet) land on exactly the same
piece of linear algebra. That convergence is the real argument that spinors are a
mathematical structure worth naming, not a quirk of quantum theory.

## what the experiment actually shows

Send neutral silver atoms through an inhomogeneous magnetic field and measure their
deflection. Classically, you'd expect a continuous spread of outcomes (every orientation
of a tiny bar magnet deflects by a different amount). What you actually see is *two*
spots, nothing in between. That's the experimental fact that forces angular momentum —
specifically, the un-paired electron's intrinsic spin — to be quantized.

## bra-ket bookkeeping

Quantum states live in an abstract vector space, written as kets $|\psi\rangle$, with
Hermitian conjugates (bras) $\langle\psi|$. Born's rule says the probability of measuring
a system prepared in state $|a\rangle$ to collapse into state $|b\rangle$ is

$$
P(a \to b) = |\langle b | a \rangle|^2.
$$

Running the Stern-Gerlach beam through a $\hat z$-oriented magnet and then a second
$\hat z$-magnet shows $|{+z}\rangle$ and $|{-z}\rangle$ are orthogonal, unit-norm states —
exactly as expected, since "up" and "down" are mutually exclusive outcomes.

## the $x$ and $y$ states are where it gets interesting

Rotate the apparatus to point along $\hat x$ and repeat: you again get two outcomes,
$|{+x}\rangle$ and $|{-x}\rangle$, each orthogonal and unit-norm. But now feed a
$|{+x}\rangle$ beam into a $\hat z$-oriented magnet, and you get a $50/50$ split. Born's
rule then pins down

$$
|{+x}\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|{+z}\rangle + |{-z}\rangle\big), \qquad
|{-x}\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|{+z}\rangle - |{-z}\rangle\big).
$$

Repeating along $\hat y$ forces complex coefficients — real numbers alone can't give a
second pair of states that's simultaneously $50/50$ against $z$ *and* orthogonal to the
$x$-states already claimed:

$$
|{+y}\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|{+z}\rangle + i|{-z}\rangle\big), \qquad
|{-y}\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|{+z}\rangle - i|{-z}\rangle\big).
$$

Lay these six states side by side with the six Jones vectors $H,V,D,A,L,R$ from the
optics chapter and the dictionary is exact, component for component. That's not a loose
analogy — the underlying linear algebra doesn't know or care which physical system it's
describing.

## why $U(2)$ is "too big" here as well

Just as with Jones vectors, rotating a spin state with a unitary matrix leaves Born's
rule probabilities unchanged if the matrix is multiplied by an overall phase — the phase
exits the inner product via the bra's complex conjugation and squares away to $1$. So
$U(2)$ over-describes the physical rotations, and we again cut the redundancy by
demanding $\det U = 1$, landing on $SU(2)$ as the group that rotates spin states around
the **Bloch sphere** (the quantum-mechanics name for the same sphere optics calls the
Poincaré sphere).

The payoff is the same angle-doubling as before, but now it's worth stating in the
language this book is named after: physical rotations in 3D space form $SO(3)$, and the
matrices that correctly transform spin-$\tfrac12$ states form $SU(2)$. The map
$SU(2) \to SO(3)$ that sends a spinor rotation to the physical rotation it induces is
exactly two-to-one — both $U$ and $-U$ in $SU(2)$ produce the same rotation in $SO(3)$,
for the same reason $\mathbf{J}$ and $-\mathbf{J}$ represent the same polarization.
$SU(2)$ is the **double cover** of $SO(3)$. Everything in this chapter and the last one
is the two-to-one covering map, worked out by hand in a specific low-dimensional case
before we have the Lie-theory language to say it in one line.
